propositions.text: The Appellant is an Indian citizen fearing her brother-in-law and family members supporting him, and makes a sur place claim based on Khalistan support.
propositions.quote: The Appellant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of India who allegedly fears her brother-in-law and several other family members who support him. She also makes a sur place claim based on her support for the Khalistan movement since arriving in Canada.

propositions.text: The RPD denied the claim on February 17, 2020, finding lack of credibility and an internal flight alternative in Mumbai.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denied her claim in a decision dated February 17, 2020, after finding that she lacks credibility and has an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Mumbai.

propositions.text: The Appellant appeals the RPD decision to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).
propositions.quote: She appeals the RPD's decision to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellant is an Indian citizen fearing family members and making a sur place claim; the RPD denied her claim for lack of credibility and IFA; she appeals to the RAD.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed and the matter is referred back to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel.
propositions.quote: The appeal is allowed. The matter is referred back to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal and refers the matter back to the RPD for redetermination by a different panel.

propositions.text: The Appellant is a 32-year-old woman from New Delhi alleging sexual advances and threats by her brother-in-law from 2010 to 2018.
propositions.quote: The Appellant is a 32-year-old woman from New Delhi who alleges that her brother-in-law was making inappropriate sexual advances and threatening her.

propositions.text: Her mother and brother assisted the brother-in-law and even visited her home after she left India.
propositions.quote: Her mother and brother were assisting her brother-in-law, and even attended her home after she left India to inquire about her.

propositions.text: She left India for Canada in 2018 and filed her refugee claim on September 9, 2018.
propositions.quote: She left India for Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, and filed her claim for refugee protection on September 9, 2018.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellant alleges sexual threats by her brother-in-law, family support for him, left India in 2018, and filed a refugee claim.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges developing interest in the Khalistan movement after arriving in Canada and involvement with Sikhs for Justice and Sikh Referendum 2020.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also alleges that she developed an interest in the Khalistan movement after arriving in Canada, which seeks an independent Sikh state in Punjab, and became involved with the group "Sikhs for Justice" and their Sikh Referendum 2020 initiative.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellant alleges involvement with the Khalistan movement and Sikh Referendum 2020 after arriving in Canada.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits new evidence including identity card, family photo, voter registration, and news articles on Khalistan and Covid-19 in India.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits proposed new evidence which includes her father's identity card listing all family members, a family photograph with her brother-in-law, her registration to vote in the Khalistan Referendum 2020, numerous news articles on the Khalistan movement and the referendum, and several news articles on the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic in India.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant submits new evidence including identity documents, family photo, voter registration, and news articles on Khalistan and Covid-19.

propositions.text: New evidence is admissible before RAD only if it arose after claim rejection, was not reasonably available, or could not reasonably be presented earlier.
propositions.quote: New evidence is only admissible before the RAD if it arose after the rejection of the claims, if it was not reasonably available, or if the Appellant could not have reasonably been expected in the circumstances to have presented the evidence at the time of the rejection of the claims.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal requires new evidence to be relevant, new, and credible for admissibility.
propositions.quote: In addition to these legislative requirements, under the Federal Court of Appeal decisions in Singh and Raza, admissibility is limited to evidence that is relevant, new, and credible.

propositions.text: The appeal is granted without considering new evidence, which would not allow substituting the determination instead of referral back to RPD.
propositions.quote: Regardless of whether the evidence meets the legislative and common law requirements, the question of its admissibility is moot because the appeal is granted without consideration of this evidence. None of this evidence would allow me to substitute my determination rather than refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: The court states new evidence admissibility rules and grants the appeal without considering new evidence, referring back to RPD instead.

propositions.text: Issues on appeal: whether RPD erred in credibility assessment, IFA finding, and failure to consider sur place claim.
propositions.quote: The issues on appeal are whether the RPD erred in its assessment of the Appellant's credibility, in its finding that she has a viable IFA in Mumbai, and whether it failed to consider her sur place claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies issues: RPD's errors on credibility, IFA, and sur place claim consideration.

propositions.text: Standard of correctness applies to RAD appeals per Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica.
propositions.quote: The standard of correctness applies to this appeal as set out by the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica.

propositions.text: RAD must independently assess refugee claim to determine correctness of RPD findings.
propositions.quote: This requires an independent assessment of the refugee claim to determine whether the RPD was correct in its findings and determinations.

propositions.text: Deference to RPD on fact or mixed fact-law issues only if RPD has meaningful advantage, which is absent here.
propositions.quote: While deference can be afforded to the RPD on specific issues when it enjoys a meaningful advantage over the RAD in making findings of fact or mixed fact and law, such an advantage does not arise in the present case.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of correctness applies, requiring independent assessment, with no deference to RPD here.

propositions.text: The RPD erred in assessing the Appellant's credibility and failed to consider her sur place claim.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred in its assessment of her credibility and failed to consider her sur place claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD erred on credibility assessment and sur place claim consideration.

propositions.text: RPD's adverse credibility findings based on lack of documentary evidence of agents of harm and family members, including birth and marriage certificates.
propositions.quote: The RPD's adverse credibility findings are based primarily on the lack of documentary evidence establishing the identity of the agents of harm and the Appellant's family members, including their birth and marriage certificates.

propositions.text: RPD disbelieved the existence of the sister and brother-in-law due to lack of documentary proof.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the panel disbelieves that [...] lived in India and was the claimant's brother-in-law as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the appellant not credible due to lack of documentary evidence of family and agents of harm.

propositions.text: Claimants are not required to provide corroboration unless there is a valid reason to question credibility, per Federal Court in Pooya.
propositions.quote: Going back to first principles, XXXX claimants are not required to provide XXXX XXXX unless there are valid reasons to question a claimant's credibility.

propositions.text: Sworn testimony presumed true unless reason to doubt, per Maldonado.
propositions.quote: This is because when a XXXX claimant swears the truth of certain allegations, there is a presumption that those allegations are true, unless there is reason to doubt their truthfulness (Maldonado v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1980] 2 FC 302 at para 5, [1979] FCJ No 248 (QL) (CA) [Maldonado]).

paragraphs.summary: The court states claimants need not provide corroboration unless credibility is questioned; sworn testimony presumed true unless doubted.

propositions.text: RPD incorrectly impugned credibility based on lack of corroboration without first having reason to question credibility.
propositions.quote: The RPD cited the principle from Maldonado... but incorrectly proceeded to impugn her testimony based on the lack of corroborative evidence without first having a reason to question her credibility.

propositions.text: No general requirement for corroboration; credibility cannot be based on absence of corroboration alone, per Ndjavera.
propositions.quote: there is no general requirement for corroboration and a panel cannot make a credibility finding based on the absence of XXXX XXXX alone.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD erred by doubting credibility due to lack of corroboration without reason to question it.

propositions.text: RPD wrongly found letters and affidavit fraudulent due to lack of identity documents and prevalence of fraudulent documents in India.
propositions.quote: The RPD also incorrectly impugned the Appellant's credibility and found that several letters and an affidavit were fraudulent because they did not include identity documents from the authors, and because the evidence in the National Documentation Package for India (NDP), indicates that certain documents can be manufactured.

propositions.text: Prevalence of fraudulent documents in home country alone insufficient to find document fraudulent without specific evidence, per Federal Court.
propositions.quote: This is contrary to Federal Court jurisprudence that the prevalence of fraudulent documents in a claimant's home country is not a sufficient basis on its own to find that a document is fraudulent in the absence of evidence that brings its authenticity into question in the specific case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD wrongly deemed documents fraudulent without specific evidence, contrary to Federal Court jurisprudence.

propositions.text: RPD failed to consider the Appellant's sur place claim despite it being raised and allowed to submit documents.
propositions.quote: The RPD erred by failing to consider the Appellant's sur place claim and her alleged fear stemming from her activities in Canada on the Sikh Referendum 2020 initiative.

propositions.text: RPD allowed submission of additional documents but did not address sur place claim in decision.
propositions.quote: Despite informing the Appellant that "I don't allow normally to do this, but I am allowing you to submit whatever other documents you wish to submit," the RPD did not address the sur place claim in its decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD failed to consider the sur place claim despite allowing document submissions.

propositions.text: Appellant believed her activities at Brampton Gurudwara came to attention of Indian authorities, though RPD did not question this.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that "she believed that her activities in which she took part at the Gurudwara (Sikh Temple) in Brampton, Ontario, came to the attention of the Indian authorities," although the RPD did not question her about whether her activities came to the attention of the authorities in India, and instead focused on the omission of the sur place claim from the BOC.

propositions.text: Sur place claim analysis focuses on whether activities abroad might cause negative reaction by home authorities and risk persecution, per Ngongo and Eshetie.
propositions.quote: The analytical framework for assessing a sur place claim was outlined by the Federal Court in Ngongo: "[t]he only relevant question is whether activities abroad might give rise to a negative reaction on the part of the authorities and thus a reasonable chance of persecution in the event of return." The analysis has been described as focusing "on whether the activities of an individual abroad might give rise to a negative reaction on the part of the authorities in their home country and lead to a reasonable chance of persecution in the event of return."

propositions.text: Since RPD did not question Appellant on sur place claim, credibility and knowledge by Indian authorities cannot be assessed.
propositions.quote: Since the RPD did not question the Appellant on this issue, I cannot assess her credibility surrounding her alleged involvement in the Khalistan movement in Canada to determine whether her activities came to the attention of the Indian authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant says her activities came to Indian authorities' attention; court notes RPD did not question her, so credibility cannot be assessed.

propositions.text: Viability of IFA cannot be assessed without first assessing credibility of sur place claim and knowledge by Indian authorities.
propositions.quote: Nor can I assess the viability of an IFA without first assessing the credibility of the Appellant's sur place claim.

propositions.text: Credibility of sur place claim and knowledge by Indian authorities are central to IFA analysis as they determine if agents of harm include state actors.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's credibility surrounding her sur place claim and the question of whether her activities became known to the Indian authorities are central issues in the first part of the IFA analysis since they would determine whether the agents of harm include state actors.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds IFA viability depends on assessing sur place claim credibility and whether Indian authorities know of her activities.

propositions.text: Cannot substitute own determination without comprehensive credibility assessment including sur place claim; referral back to RPD is appropriate remedy.
propositions.quote: I cannot substitute my own determination without a comprehensive assessment of the Appellant's credibility, including her sur place claim and the question of whether her alleged activities are known to the Indian authorities. A referral back to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel is therefore the appropriate remedy in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court cannot substitute its own decision without full credibility assessment and refers the matter back to RPD.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed and the matter is referred back to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel.
propositions.quote: The appeal is allowed. I refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal and refers the matter back to the RPD for redetermination by a different panel.
